items.text: On one rented 8-GPU machine, how much storm-forecast skill does about 60 times more compute (3 km explicit vs 12 km parameterized convection) buy, compared with radar assimilation and an ML emulator?
The 3 km WRF with explicit convection beats the 12 km WRF with parameterized convection on radar-checked storm skill, but radar assimilation matters more early on, as in Roberts & Lean 2008.
The 3 km explicit-convection WRF has a paired 95% bootstrap interval for the skill-score gain over 12 km that lies above 0, plus better timing of the daily cycle.
The interval for the 3 km minus 12 km FSS gain spans 0, as Roberts & Lean saw at 4 km [roberts_lean].

items.text: Run WRF at 12 km and 3 km on 16 central-US storm days, score both against radar, and compare with archived HRRR, a StormCast ML emulator and persistence. A paired bootstrap tests whether 60x compute buys skill.
Roberts & Lean 2008 ran the Met Office model at 12, 4 and 1 km on 10 convective days against radar; the 1 km run was most skilful, 4 km improved little on 12 km [roberts_lean].

items.page_quote: It is anticipated that the introduction of data assimilation at a high resolution will improve skill further, particularly over the first few hours when the spinup from a coarse-resolution initial state is a problem.
items.note: The 3 km vs 12 km part is a prediction and needs no source. The attribution 'radar assimilation matters more early on, as in Roberts & Lean 2008' cites no source on the card; checked against the Roberts & Lean page fetched for other items, it is only partly backed. The paper says 'The purpose was to examine the improvement to forecast skill from increased resolution alone. Data assimilation is a separate issue for subsequent papers.' What it observed is that 'The 4- and 1-km models are initially less skillful than the 12-km model, because they have not had time to spin up from the 12-km initial state' with the 1-km model overtaking 'after 1-2 h'; the 12-km run used 3DVAR, MOPS and latent heat nudging while the 4/1-km runs were initialised from it. The early-hours effect is attributed to spin-up, and a DA benefit in the first few hours is anticipated, not measured. Cite roberts_lean and soften 'as in' to 'as anticipated by'.

items.page_quote: The 4-km model performs poorly compared with the 1-km model, and shows little or no improvement on the 12-km model at any scale apart from the high-accumulation thresholds.
items.note: The prediction (interval spans 0) needs no source. The attribution 'as Roberts & Lean saw at 4 km' is loosely supported: the page says the 4-km model 'did not improve much on the 12-km model'. But Roberts & Lean reported no bootstrap or confidence interval (no occurrence of 'bootstrap' or 'confidence' in the full text; their error bars represent radar uncertainty), and the 4-km result was threshold-dependent: 'For the low thresholds of 0.2 and 1.0 mm, both the 1- and 12-km models were significantly more skillful over all scales than the 4-km model', while 'For the higher thresholds of 4.0 and 16.0 mm, the 4- and 1-km models have comparable skill, but the 12-km model is considerably worse'. The recorded quote (about the 1-km model) does not itself support the 4-km claim; the 4-km sentence above does.

items.page_quote: The Met Office Unified Model was run with grid spacings of 12, 4, and 1 km for 10 days in which convection occurred during the summers of 2003 and 2004. ... The results show that the 1-km model was the most skillful over all but the smallest scales (approximately <10-15 km). ... The 4-km model did not improve much on the 12-km model because of the difficulties of representing convection at that resolution, which was accentuated by the spinup from 12-km fields.
items.note: Every claim checks out against the abstract: Met Office Unified Model, 12/4/1 km, 10 convective days, verified against radar ('comparison of rainfall forecasts with radar using fractional coverage'), 1 km most skilful, 4 km improved little on 12 km. The recorded quote is slightly misworded ('skilful at' vs page 'skillful over') but the substance is exact.

items.text: On a synthetic benchmark fault, does earthquake-forecast skill keep rising as the assimilation ensemble grows, or does it level off early while model error and sensor depth decide?
Skill levels off at tens to hundreds of members, because model error and depth of data limit it first, as the one perfect-model study [van_dinther] suggests.
Each member's adaptive time stepping through earthquakes: thousands of steps per event, up to about 8,050 accepted steps per cycle.
Thousands of independent members run as columns of one batched matrix on GPU; finished members are gathered into smaller batches every 32 steps so slow ruptures do not stall the rest.
Skill is still rising beyond 1,024 members in the model-error or particle-filter arms, by more than the gain from deep stress data.
Skill plateaus at 256 members or fewer in every ensemble Kalman filter arm; model error or deep data changes skill more than going from 32 members to the largest.

Run thousands of copies of a benchmark earthquake fault on GPUs inside ensemble Kalman and particle filters. Measure forecast skill against ensemble size, with and without model error and deep sensors, against simple baselines [van_dinther].
van Dinther et al. 2019 ran an ensemble Kalman filter with 150 members on a 2-D subduction analogue; Diab-Montero et al. 2023 used 50 members on a single-point 1-D fault model with perfect model.
Forecast skill versus ensemble size beyond 150 members, under model error, on a depth-resolved rate-and-state fault, with EnKF compared against a large particle filter.
A single-member run of the first benchmark fault at 25 m reproduces an independent code, QDYN: recurrence interval and first-event time within 1%, slip-rate series overlay at benchmark stations.
A plateau would confirm the hypothesis only for synthetic data from a known model class, not the real Earth. GPU timings are assumptions until Phase 0b; truth noise amplitude is tuned, not observed.

items.page_quote: However, as little as 20 ensemble members are found to already capture most of the diversity within the models
items.note: Quote is verbatim on the page and the paper is confirmed as a perfect-model experiment ("We perform a perfect model experiment to test whether EDA could be used to estimate fault stresses"). But the page does not suggest skill levels off: it says "Larger ensembles typically allow for improved forecasts, so we show results for the largest number tested: 150 ensemble members", and Appendix B reports "increasing the number of ensemble members N, decreases the L1 norm as 1/sqrt(N)" with a power-law fit, i.e. continued improvement rather than a plateau. The 20-member sentence is about ensemble diversity, not forecast skill. The causal part (model error, data depth limit first) is the plan's prediction and needs no source.

scores.reason: Tests weather storm skill, not earthquake prediction; the stand-in is far from the root question, and a 3 km gain is already likely.
Axis is 60x and compute-bought, with held_fixed inputs. But noise is not compared with an expected effect size, and 16 cases may be underpowered.
Independent MRMS radar truth plus a benchmark reproduction within 2x and an HRRR scorer check; the benchmark is a different grid, so not exact.
Prior covers the UK model at 4 km and 1 km on 10 days; WRF, central US and 2024 with ML comparison remain open, and the gap is stated.
Method is none; runs are independent cases side by side, with no time-dependency removal.
restructuring.method is none, so the baseline criterion does not apply.

critique.decides_by_reason: The decision rule needs a bootstrap CI over cases of FSS(B)-FSS(A); only the p2 main runs provide enough cases. The pilot has one case.

scores.reason: Result bears on real forecasting only through a synthetic known-model step; plateau is already the more likely outcome given the prior.
Ensemble size spans 1,000x, with inputs held fixed and SE-based noise rule; but the deep-data comparison is a data change, not compute.
Hidden synthetic truth scored by Molchan area; anchor matches independent QDYN within 1%, though not a published number.
Prior reached 150 members perfect-model; plan states the gap beyond 150 under model error with a particle filter.
Independent members run side by side with compaction rebalancing; no step dependency is removed, and prior already used ensembles.
Baseline is untuned NumPy CPU, copies on same GPUs not stated, and no phase times arms to one answer.

critique.decides_by_reason: Decision rule needs skill versus ensemble size from E1-E4, which only production phase p1 produces; p0b only measures timings and verification.
